Conclusions Adequate serum vitamin D levels are related to human health. Despite a huge number of experimental and human studies documenting an increased susceptibility to diseases ranging from osteoporosis to autoimmune diseases, inflammation, infections, and cancer, the real role of vitamin D supplementation is still to be defined. Moreover, the most appropriate dosage required in different populations and patient groups, including ulcerative colitis patients, has not yet been established. What constitutes an adequate intake of vitamin K is even less well defined, resulting in different nutritional guidelines in different countries. In patients with ulcerative colitis, more so for those with inactive or mildly active disease, dietary intervention may prove to be adequate in providing enough calcium, vitamin D, and K to favor bone health and minimize the risk of osteopenia and osteoporosis. Additional advantages may reside in the anti-inflammatory activity of vitamins D and K [ ]. This is easily attained by avoiding the unnecessary restriction of dietary fiber, milk, and milk derivatives. Favoring the consumption of low-lactose cheese and lactose-free foods is helpful in patients with severe lactase deficiency. In addition to micronutrients, emerging evidence also shows that several gut microbiome metabolites, such as SCFAs, secondary BA, indole derivatives, and amines, are directly and indirectly involved in bone metabolism, although their mechanisms of action remain to be elucidated ( ). In a proportion of UC patients, and more so in those with marked disease activity, dietary counseling may prove insufficient to provide the daily requirements of vitamins and micronutrients needed for bone health. Vitamin D supplementation in association with adequate calcium intake should thus be prescribed to all IBD patients in whom dietary intake is below the RDA and in those requiring systemic corticosteroids [ , ]. Daily vitamin D (800–1000 IU) and calcium (800–1000 mg) supplements are advisable. Supplementation is also advisable in those UC patients in whom dietary vitamin K intake is low. A daily intake of 90–140 micrograms is considered adequate. This can be provided by supplementing commercially available formulations of vitamins K1, K2, or K3. Further studies are needed to define whether an adequate intake of vitamins D and K, besides reducing the risk of osteopenia and osteoporosis, will prove useful for the control of chronic inflammation in UC patients.

Introduction Primary/idiopathic hypertrophic osteoarthropathy (PHOA, pachydermoperiostosis ) is very rare in children. There are two peaks of incidence of disease symptoms – around 1 year of life and around 15 years of life. The chronic course of the disease is characterized by dynamic development of symptoms in childhood, with the relief or resolution of symptoms in adulthood. The disease is observed mainly in men (7-9 : 1 in relation to women) and more often in the black population. Family occurrence is characteristic. The life expectancy of patients with primary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy is as in the general population [ , ]. Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy is characterized by a triad of symptoms. These are: Periosteal bone formation ( periostosis ) most often of the distal parts of the shafts of long bones (mainly tibia and fibula, followed by phalanges), less often epiphyses. Periosteal bone formation may be accompanied by acroosteolysis [ - ]. Skin hypertrophy (pachydermia). Thickening of facial features, up to the formation of characteristic folds of the hairy scalp and forehead (the so-called lion’s head); hand and foot skin hypertrophy. Digital clubbing ( Hippocratic/Hippocrates fingers, drumstick fingers ). It is a characteristic thickening of the soft tissues of the distal phalanges with deformation and matting of nails ( watch-crystal nails ). In the “onset” phase, clubbed fingers can be easily seen on physical examination; they arouse patient anxiety. In the development phase of this pathology, measurements of distal phalanges and tests are helpful in the evaluation. The typical feature is the increase in the ratio of the finger circumference in the middle of the distal phalanx to the finger circumference in the area of the distal interphalangeal joint ( phalangeal depth ratio ). In the Schamroth test, in the case of healthy patients, the fingers, after applying the dorsal surfaces of the skin in the area of the distal phalanges of the fingers, create a characteristic diamond-shaped gap, which is not visible in the case of a patient with osteoarthropathy. For measurement description and schemes see [ ]. The dominant clinical symptoms in the course of osteoarthropathy in a large percentage of patients (20-40% [ ]), especially in the initial stage of the disease, are pain and other features of arthritis, i.e. swelling, reduced mobility and morning stiffness [ , - ]. During the diagnosis of primary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy, attention should also be paid to other characteristic pathologies that may occur in patients. These include increased foot and hand size, seborrhoea, hyperhidrosis, ptosis, delayed closure of cranial sutures/fontanelles, presence of intrasutural bones ( ossiculae intersuturae, Wormian bones ), and patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). In some patients, the hypertrophy of the periosteum “inwards”, i.e. towards the marrow cavities ( endoperiostosis ), may lead to bone marrow fibrosis and thus impair haematopoiesis up to pancytopenia [ - ]. It should be noted that in many patients the clinical picture of primary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy is incomplete [ ]. The sequence in which the characteristic symptoms, mentioned above, appear also varies, which hinders the diagnosis of the disease [ ]. We observe people with only clubbed fingers, and on the other hand, patients with haematological disorders suffering from painful deformities of the joints with impaired functionality and disfiguring hypertrophy of the scalp and face. However, the known causes of hypertrophic osteoarthropathy seem to explain well the observed symptoms and significant phenotypic differences found in individual patients. Mutations in genes related to the metabolism and transport of prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) cause primary/idiopathic hypertrophic osteoarthropathy. Those are the HPGD gene encoding PGE2 metabolising enzyme and the SCLO2A1 gene encoding PGE2 transport membrane protein. These gene mutations cause increased PGE2 in serum. Increased concentrations of this mediator induce the activity of osteoblasts and fibroblasts, which leads to increased production of collagen and other proteins of the extracellular matrix. PGE2 has also been postulated to influence bone tissue by interacting with the nervous regulation of bone homeostasis [ ]. Mutations of genes associated with PGE2 metabolism and transport may be transmitted by autosomal recessive or dominant inheritance, but also show incomplete penetrance [ ]. Mutations of individual genes seem to be associated with different clinical pictures of the disease. The manifestation of symptoms in early childhood is associated with a mutation in the HPGD gene (PGE2 metabolising enzyme), with disturbances in the cranial sutures. Mutations of the gene for the PGE2 transport membrane protein, i.e. SLCO2A1 , lead to the development of more severe hypertrophic osteoarthropathy in late childhood/early adulthood with skin hypertrophy and bone marrow fibrosis. Gastrointestinal complaints in the course of hypertrophic osteoarthropathy also seem to be associated with the latter mutation, including ulcers, polyps, and hypertrophic gastritis [ , ]. All this explains the family occurrence of the disease and finding different disease phenotypes in individual patients with the primary form of hypertrophic osteoarthropathy. Indirect evidence

Secondary form of hypertrophic osteoarthropathy Confirmation of the presence of osteoarthropathy features, as listed above, in a patient requires a thorough differential diagnosis, due to the fact that the vast majority of patients with osteoarthropathy are patients with a secondary form of the disease (95-97%). Careful history and additional tests in a child with clinical signs of osteoarthropathy should exclude chronic heart diseases (cyanotic heart defects and blood vessel defects), respiratory system diseases (cystic fibrosis, chronic or recurrent lower respiratory tract infections, interstitial lung diseases), and neoplastic diseases (including lung metastases). The incidence, course and mortality in cases of secondary osteoarthropathy depend on the cause, while treatment of the underlying disease alleviates or completely resolves the symptoms [ ]. In children, secondary causes of osteoarthropathy are relatively less common than in adults [ ]. In adults the causes of the secondary osteoarthropathy include neoplastic tumours, infections, chronic inflammation, and chronic hypoxia [ ]. The typical causes are chest tumours (non-small cell lung cancer, pleural cancer, thymoma, neoplastic metastases) [ ], tumours of the haematopoietic system, cyanotic heart defects, blood vessel defects, vasculitis (including polyarteritis nodosa), endocarditis, respiratory tract defects, pulmonary fibrosis, inflammatory bowel disease [ ], cirrhosis, congenital anaemia (mainly thalassaemia), thyroid disease (mainly Graves’ disease), medications (including voriconazole, retinoids), and venous insufficiency of the lower extremities [ - ]. In practice, in adults, osteoarthropathy is in most cases caused by pathology of the respiratory system (90%). Due to its high correlation with thoracic tumours (4-17% of patients with non-small cell lung cancer), it can be considered a paraneoplastic symptom which occurs even several months before the diagnosis of the underlying disease [ ]. In 2 patients radiological imaging revealed acro-osteolytic lesions of the bones of the feet. Discussion Primary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy is relatively simple to diagnose, when the characteristic picture of the disease is complete. However, the description of paediatric cases from the Paediatric Rheumatology Department presented in this study confirms the difficulties with diagnosing children with primary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy described in the literature, which is related to the incomplete clinical picture of the disease and the dominant osteoarticular complaints at clinical evaluation [ , ]. Only one patient (patient No. 3) had all the typical symptoms from the characteristic triad of primary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy, i.e. digital clubbing, skin hypertrophy and periosteal bone formation in the bone shaft in X-ray examinations. Moreover, in this child other symptoms of the disease were observed, such as seborrhoea, hyperhidrosis, and disorders of the fontanelle and cranial suture closure. In another boy (patient No. 5) except for the digital clubbing, only skin hypertrophy was found as regards the classic triad of symptoms. In all patients, digital clubbing was accompanied by at least one characteristic “additional feature” of the disease, i.e. hyperhidrosis (in 4 out of 5), seborrhoea (in 2 out of 5), or abnormal fontanelle/cranial suture closure (in 2 out of 5). Clinical features of arthritis were found in 3 out of 5 children: joint swelling with limitation of joint mobility. In the remaining two patients, only one of these features, i.e. swelling or limited mobility, was observed. In two patients, the features of thickening/overgrowth of the synovial membrane were confirmed by imaging. It is known that the dominant clinical symptoms in the course of osteoarthropathy in a large percentage of patients (20-40% [ ]), especially in the initial stage of the disease, are pain and other features of arthritis, i.e. swelling, limited mobility and morning stiffness [ , - ]. Joint complaints most often occur in symmetrical joints, especially knee joints, ankle joints, wrist joints and finger joints [ ]. The most characteristic are joint cavity effusions found on physical examination and imaging examinations [ , , , , ]. The synovial fluid shows features of non-specific inflammation [ ]. It is known that the features of arthritis found in patients, as often the first and dominant symptom of hypertrophic osteoarthropathy, may lead to erroneous diagnosis of systemic connective tissue diseases [ ]. There have been reports of patients in whom primary or secondary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy was finally confirmed, and who had previously diagnosed and unsuccessfully treated systemic connective tissue disease due to the features of arthritis – among others, reactive arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, and systemic lupus erythematosus [ , ]. For the same reason, hypertrophic osteoarthropathy can mimic the symptoms of juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) [ ] and thus lead to unnecessary treatment, including immunosuppressive therapy. There are reports in the literature of at least 5 cases of children whose diagnosis of JIA was revised and treatment was discontinued, including immunosuppressive therapy, due to the diagnosis of primary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy [ , , ]. In their paper, Giancane et al . [ ] presented patients who were given long-term JIA treatment (NSAIDs, synovectomy, intra-articular steroid administration, immunosuppressive treatment with sulfasalazine and methotrexate, and in one case also tumor necrosis factor (TNF) antagonists – etanercept and adalimumab) and whose JIA diagnosis was withdrawn due to the occurrence of further typical symptoms of the underlying disease, confirmed by genetic testing. Side effects of NSAID therapy administered for misdiagnosed JIA in a patient with primary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy have also been reported [ ]. One of the patients treated in our department (patient No. 1), due to the features of arthritis, was diagnosed with JIA in the past and was unsuccessfully treated for several years, initially with methotrexate, then with methotrexate in combination with sulfasalazine. All of them were examined because of pain and features of arthritis. We observed an incomplete clinical picture of the disease. One patient required a revision of the previous diagnosis of JIA and discontinuation of ineffective treatment with disease-modifying drugs (DMARDs). Key Summary Points Introduction Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) is a common inflammatory rheumatic disease primarily involving the periarticular structures of proximal joints that occurs almost exclusively in those over 50 years of age [ ]. The clinical spectrum of PMR is wide; however, it classically manifests as bilateral pain and stiffness of the shoulder, neck and pelvic girdle, each with an early morning preponderance [ ]. PMR was traditionally considered as a relatively benign clinical condition, characterised by a rapid response to glucocorticoid (GC) therapy and a presumed self-limiting disease course. However, there is a growing recognition of its substantial impact on patients, including significant disability and a marked reduction in health-related quality of life (HRQoL) [ – ]. Adding to its complexity, PMR demonstrates considerable heterogeneity in both clinical presentation and disease progression [ – ]. The absence of a gold standard diagnostic test, coupled with a wide range of potential disease mimics, presents substantial diagnostic challenges, even with specialist expertise. The overarching aim of treatment in PMR is to restore a patient’s HRQoL by providing sustained symptomatic relief with suppression of the underlying systemic inflammation and prevention of disease relapse, whilst minimising treatment-associated adverse effects [ ]. Despite considerable progress in understanding the pathophysiology of PMR over the past decade, GCs remain the mainstay of therapy. Although GCs are extremely efficacious initially, disease relapses are common, and treatment frequently extends beyond 5 years [ ]. This results in high cumulative GC burdens for many, with associated toxicity, which is of particular concern, especially in this older and more vulnerable cohort of patients. The need for alternative, effective and safe GC-sparing agents is readily apparent. The pivotal SAPHYR study has resulted in the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval of the first biologic therapy in PMR, sarilumab, for those with refractory PMR [ ]. This has ushered in a new era in PMR management, with an increasing number of biologic therapies currently under evaluation in randomised controlled trials (RCTs) [ ]. The incorporation of these new agents into the therapeutic algorithm of PMR, however, underscores several shortcomings in our current management approach. Whilst PMR has until recently been diagnosed and managed in primary care, with only refractory or difficult cases referred for specialist evaluation [ ], there is now growing interest in the utility and feasibility of rapid access pathways and early specialist involvement in all cases of suspected PMR as a means to facilitate timely diagnosis, identification of a concomitant giant cell arteritis (GCA), enable disease stratification and appropriate treatment initiation. Furthermore, the evidence base for disease monitoring in PMR remains limited. There is a pressing need for a standardised consensus on the definitions of relapse and remission, as well as the development of structured monitoring strategies to optimise patient care and outcomes. In this article, we provide an overview of the evidence to date on current management strategies in isolated PMR, encompassing diagnostic approaches and both non-pharmacological and pharmacological therapeutic options. Finally, we discuss the unmet needs in the existing care paradigm and propose directions for future management strategies. This article is therefore based on previously conducted studies and does not contain any new studies with human participants or animals performed by any of the authors. Accordingly, its care has been primarily executed in the hands of non-specialists, with referral to secondary care reserved for those with relapsing or refractory disease, or those with GC-related adverse events [ ]. This is further amplified by the lack of a gold standard definitive diagnostic test, with diagnosis based on symptoms, signs and the evaluation of the acute phase reactants C-reactive protein (CRP) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). Whilst musculoskeletal ultrasound (MSUS) is increasingly employed, there is no definitive diagnostic finding, and not all centres have the desired level of MSUS expertise necessary. Other imaging techniques, such as positron emission tomography–computed tomography (PET-CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) show promise; however, they have yet to be adopted into routine clinical practice [ ]. Moreover, a reported 15–20% of those with PMR have a concomitant GCA, either at disease onset or throughout the course of their disease [ , ]. The British Society of Rheumatology (BSR) guidelines for the management of PMR [ ] and, more recently, the international PMR/GCA study group [ ] recommend specialist evaluation in each case of isolated PMR, with rapid access strategies recommended in those with severe symptoms [ ]. Given the ability of GC to mask laboratory and imaging findings which may be useful in both the diagnosis and prognostication of those with isolated PMR, their commencement should ideally be deferred until after specialist review [ ]. However, active, untreated PMR has a profound impact on a patient’s function and HRQoL, and therefore, delaying the instigation of GC is only possible if there are expedited referral pathways such as “fast-track clinics” in place. The use of fast-track clinics in GCA has been widely reported, with benefits including rapid and accurate diagnosis, early initiation of appropriate therapy, reduced risk of complications including permanent visual loss, in addition to overall increased cost-effectiveness vs. standard care [ – ]. To date, three studies have reported on the use of fast-track clinics in PMR, with each supporting their role in delivering timely, accessible specialist care resulting in enhanced diagnostic accuracy and overall patient outcomes [ , , ]. Patients assessed through the fast-track clinics experienced a shorter time to PMR diagnosis, a reduction in total inpatient hospital days [ , ], and a reduced starting dose of prednisolone compared to those managed by standard care [ , , ]. Furthermore, the implementation of fast-track clinics appears to be more cost-effective by lowering the annual cost for patients [ ]. However, the feasibility of the implementation of a fast-track PMR clinic relies on national and local resources, and with an already strained rheumatology workforce, and long waiting lists, coupled with our aging population, additional resources would need to be assigned to PMR to ensure the successful implementation of such initiatives. Further studies, in particular, RCTs, and cost-effectiveness analyses need to be undertaken to address the precise role of the rheumatologist in the care of those with isolated PMR. However, with the expanding number of GC-sparing agents on the horizon, that only rheumatologists can prescribe, there will likely be an inevitable move away from general practitioner-led management. Treat-to-Target and Disease Monitoring The recently published treat-to-target (T2T) recommendations for GCA and PMR developed by an international multidisciplinary task force suggest regular monitoring of those with PMR, as frequently as every 1–4 weeks until remission is achieved [ ]. The taskforce recommend that disease severity, patient comorbidities and potential predictors of adverse disease outcomes should guide treatment selection [ ]. Whilst the 2015 European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) and American College of Rheumatology (ACR) recommendations for PMR management identify female sex, high acute phase reactants and peripheral arthritis as associated with worse disease outcomes and increased risk of relapse [ ], the overall data in the literature surrounding prognostic markers is conflicting and inconsistent. The disease course of PMR can be highly heterogenous, and at present there is no means of accurately stratifying from the outset who will experience recurrent relapses, GC dependence and overall worse disease outcomes, including severe GC complications. As the therapeutic armamentarium of PMR expands, the ability to predict disease course and risk stratify patients is an area garnering increased scientific attention. The development of a disease stratification tool would enable personalised treatment from the time of diagnosis, with the potential to transform disease outcomes, whilst limiting unnecessary toxicity. A major obstacle in defining a treatment target is the lack of an international consensus on the definitions of disease response, remission and relapse. This has resulted in a marked heterogeneity and inconsistency in the definitions used to define disease activity and outcomes in clinical studies [ , ], which results in significant limitations not only in the interpretation of findings but also in the ability to inform the optimal disease activity monitoring approaches in clinical practice. Current monitoring strategies in PMR consist primarily of a clinician-based assessment and the evaluation of traditional inflammatory markers, namely ESR and CRP. This strategy is inherently problematic considering that symptoms may be non-specific during disease relapse, with multiple potential differential diagnoses and disease mimics. Additionally, normal CRP or ESR values have been observed in up to 17% and 27% of relapses, respectively [ ]. Moreover, this approach has limited value in those prescribed interleukin-6 (IL-6) antagonists with their associated neutralisation of both ESR and CRP. In an attempt to address this, the PMR activity score (PMR-AS) was first published in 2004 [ ], and has undergone a number of iterations since then including the development of the PMR-AS-CRP [ ]. This composite score of five parameters includes pain, assessed using a visual analogue scale (VASp); physician global assessment assessed using a visual analogue scale (VASph); morning stiffness in minutes (MS); physical function assessed by elevation of the upper limb assessed by active shoulder abduction ranging from 0 to 3 (EUL); and finally CRP (mg/dL) [ ]. Thresholds have been defined for PMR disease remission (< 1.5), medium disease activity (7–17) and high disease activity (> 17). In clinical trials and studies, PMR-AS is a commonly employed instrument for disease activity assessment [ ], and indeed it is the only validated composite score for monitoring disease activity in patients with PMR. However, despite its increasing use in research studies and trials, a COSMIN-based systematic review demonstrated the current paucity of information on certain measurement properties, including structural validity and internal consistency, which may have significant implications for its clinical applicability [ ]. Other outcomes such as MSUS, MRI and PET-CT imaging have been explored; however, imaging findings are impacted by the commencement of treatment, and have a low responsiveness to change once established on therapy [ , ]. These methods are also limited by accessibility, expertise and financial cost. Whilst Outcome Measures in Rheumatology (OMERACT) projects are currently ongoing to define remission, relapse and refractory disease in PMR [ ], there is a significant unmet need to identify novel methods of disease activity assessment and monitoring. Accurate identification of disease relapse is essential for clinicians to prevent unnecessary exposure to potentially harmful immunosuppressive agents in the absence of a disease relapse, while also ensuring timely intervention where appropriate to avoid suboptimal disease control. The T2T recommendations suggest that all patients with PMR, and their caregivers, should receive information pertaining to PMR clinical disease features, treatment-related benefits and adverse effects, comorbidities and potential complications [ ]. Patients with PMR tend to be chronologically older, and show signs of accelerated aging with a higher prevalence of geriatric syndromes including sarcopenia and frailty [ ]. The ubiquitous use of GCs and their impact on muscle mass is likely contributory. This presents unique challenges that underscore the importance of a holistic approach to PMR care, with multidisciplinary care and geriatric principles at the helm [ ]. Additionally, addressing the burden of polypharmacy in this older, comorbid population and implementing “deprescribing” to improve medication use where appropriate is essential to reduce adverse effects, drug–drug interactions and drug–disease interactions [ ]. Therapeutic Agents in PMR Glucocorticoids GCs have been the mainstay of PMR treatment for decades. Whilst there is no evidence-based, standardised protocol for steroid taper, the 2015 EULAR/ACR recommendation suggests starting with a prednisone dose equivalent (PDE) between 12.5 and 25 mg per day [ ]. The specific dose chosen within this range is primarily physician-led and patient-specific, tailored to comorbidities, likelihood of GC-related adverse events and risk of relapse. Characteristically, patients experience a profound and rapid resolution in their symptomatology upon introduction of GCs. Once remission is achieved, GCs should be tapered gradually; however, the optimal tapering strategy remains controversial largely because of the paucity of studies addressing it [ ]. Previously, isolated PMR was considered a relatively “mild” condition, with most patients anticipated to complete their GC course within a 12-month period. However, we now recognise that for a significant majority of patients, their disease course is marked by frequent relapses and subsequent huge GC burdens over a number of years [ , , ]. Indeed, a meta-analysis of observational studies reported the pooled proportions of individuals still using GCs at 1, 2, and 5 years were 77% (95% CI 71–83%), 51% (95% CI 41–61%), and 25% (95% CI 15–36%), respectively [ ]. Data from the ACR Rheumatology Informatics System for Effectiveness (RISE) registry reported 63.8% of those with PMR remained on GCs at 12–24 months, of whom only 39% were prescribed a GC-sparing agent [ ]. This long-term use of GCs is suboptimal, and highlights the significant shortcomings in our current management paradigm of isolated PMR. Moreover, those with PMR are typically older, frailer [ ] and so more vulnerable to the well-recognised adverse effects of GC therapy. Up to 85% of patients with PMR experience at least one GC-associated adverse effect [ , ]. This substantial GC-related toxicity coupled with the high relapse rate underscores the urgent need for effective GC-sparing therapies. Despite this, currently no pharmacotherapeutics apart from GCs are recommended as stand-alone first-line treatments in isolated PMR. Musculoskeletal effects include GC-induced myopathy and reduced bone mineral density (BMD) with osteoporosis and fragility fractures. GC-related myopathy typically affects the proximal skeletal muscles and is characterised by pain-free weakness and muscle atrophy which affects physical performance. It can be difficult to differentiate clinically from symptoms of PMR and its many disease mimics. EULAR recommends that GC-related muscle weakness should be assessed “through questioning” at the start and end of treatment in clinical trials [ ]. We advocate that in addition to enquiring about typical steroid myopathy symptoms (difficulty climbing stairs, raising from a chair or lifting objects) at each clinic visit, patient education on the importance of exercise initiatives be emphasised, with proactive early referral to physiotherapy as appropriate. BMD decreases even with low dose GCs and there is an increased risk of osteoporosis and fractures with higher GC doses and cumulative GC burden [ , ]. There is substantial morbidity and associated healthcare costs associated with fractures, particularly in older adults. It is important to note, however, that although GCs contribute significantly to reduced BMD, the aetiopathogenesis of osteoporosis is typically multifactorial in PMR and indeed other inflammatory rheumatic diseases [ ]. Systemic inflammation associated with poorly controlled disease activity, low physical activity, poor nutrition, older age and hormonal loss secondary to menopause all negatively impact bone health [ ]. Therefore, optimisation of these factors and a multimodal approach to osteoporosis management is essential. The ACR guidelines for the prevention and treatment of GC-induced osteoporosis recommend that all adults ≥ 40 years of age, which is representative of all patients with PMR, should have their fracture risk estimated using the fracture risk assessment tool (FRAX), and undergo BMD testing within 6 months of the initial GC treatment [ ]. Every 12 months, fracture risk should be reassessed, and BMD retesting should be performed every 1–3 years if not on osteoporosis prophylaxis, or every 2–3 years if established on osteoporosis prophylaxis therapy, outside of calcium and vitamin D [ ]. All patients with PMR (women ≥ 40 years old, and men ≥ 40 years who are at moderate to high risk of fracture) should be treated with an oral bisphosphonate [ ]. Disease-Modifying Anti-rheumatic Drugs Conventional Synthetic Disease-Modifying Anti-rheumatic Drugs The efficacy of conventional synthetic disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (csDMARDs) in isolated PMR remains uncertain, with studies yielding inconsistent findings. The most studied, and indeed used csDMARD, is methotrexate (MTX) [ ]. Its clinical efficacy in the management of PMR has been reported in three RCTs, albeit with mixed results [ – ]. Two of the studies demonstrated the efficacy of MTX [ , ], whereas the third failed to show any GC-sparing benefit [ ]. The studies supporting the efficacy of MTXs were of higher methodological quality; however, the total number of patients investigated in the RCTs is low ( n = 194). Notably, only low dosages of MTX, equivalent to or less than 10 mg, were evaluated in these trial populations, and one may therefore postulate that a higher dosage would yield alternative findings. The results of a multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, “PMR MODE” (NL8366), assessing the efficacy of MTX at a dose of 25 mg per week in addition to a 24-week prednisolone taper are highly anticipated to answer this question [ ]. Moreover, the “STERLING-PMR” (ISRCTN17828080) trial examining the role of MTX and leflunomide (LEF) in patients with PMR who have experienced at least one disease relapse is currently ongoing. It is a phase 3 open-labelled RCT comparing standard care plus MTX (starting dose of 15 mg, progressively increased to 25 mg, or reduced to 10 mg if not tolerated) or LEF if MTX is not effective or not tolerated. Despite the conflicting results and lack of clear evidence showing any true reduction in GC-related adverse events, the 2015 EULAR/ACR recommendations include a conditional recommendation to consider the early incorporation of MTX with a GC regimen in those at increased risk of GC-related adverse events or prolonged disease course [ ]. Moreover, these recommendations also recommend MTX in those experiencing relapse with an inadequate response to GC or GC-related adverse events on follow-up [ ]. The recent French Society of Rheumatology guidelines for the management of PMR also recommend MTX as an alternative to IL-6 inhibitors in GC-dependent PMR [ ]. Until recently, the role of LEF as a GC-sparing agent in refractory PMR was supported only by two case series [ , ]. However, a multicentre observational study by Vinicki et al. compared the use of MTX ( n = 143; median dose 15 mg/week) and LEF ( n = 43; 20 mg/day fixed dose) as GC-sparing agents, and reported the superiority of LEF for achieving remission and GC discontinuation ( p = 0.001) [ ]. Furthermore, the time until GC discontinuation was shorter in the LEF group (median 4.7 months) versus the MTX group (median 31.8 months) ( p < 0.001) [ ]. Although this fosters promise for the use of LEF in refractory PMR, several important limitations must be considered. These include its non-randomised design, the lack of a specified GC starting dose or tapering regimen (which was left to the treating physicians discretion), and the higher CRP and ESR levels in the MTX group at baseline and at the time of enrolment suggesting potentially greater disease activity. Additionally, a large number of patients in the MTX group received doses of 15 mg or less, which may represent underdosing and could have contributed to its apparent inferiority [ ]. Biologic Disease-Modifying Anti-rheumatic Drugs Interleukin-6 Antagonists Given the pivotal role of interleukin-6 (IL-6) in the pathogenesis of PMR, and the consistently elevated levels of serum IL-6 levels in those with active disease [ ], the exploration of the efficacy of IL-6 antagonists in PMR has ushered in a new era in the management of PMR. Following the positive results of the pivotal SAPHYR study ( NCT03600818 ), sarilumab, a fully human anti-IL-6 receptor alpha monoclonal antibody, was approved for the management of refractory PMR by the FDA in 2023 [ ]. This phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT evaluated the efficacy and safety of subcutaneously administered sarilumab in 118 patients with active GC-refractory PMR on 7.5 mg/day prednisolone [ ]. A significantly higher number of patients in the sarilumab group (200 mg every 2 weeks, with 14-week GC taper) compared with the comparator group (placebo every 2 weeks with 52-week GC taper) achieved sustained remission from weeks 12 to 52 (28.3% vs. 10.3%; p = 0.0193) [ ]. Additionally, at week 52, the cumulative GC burden was significantly lower in the sarilumab (777 mg) vs. placebo group (2044 mg) ( p < 0.001), with the GTI also favouring the sarilumab group [97 (76–121.5)] compared with the placebo group [112.5 (85–141)] [ ]. The most commonly reported adverse event during sarilumab treatment was neutropenia, which occurred in 15% of patients and resulted in treatment discontinuation in 12% [ ]. Notably, no infections were associated with the neutropenia. However, white blood cell counts should be carefully monitored in those treated with sarilumab, with dose adjustment or cessation of therapy as appropriate, should neutropenia occur. Tocilizumab, an IL-6 receptor antagonist, has also had positive outcomes in two phase 3 trials [ , ]. The SEMAPHORE study ( NCT02908217 ), a phase 3, double-blind, parallel-group, placebo-controlled RCT, examined the efficacy of intravenously administered tocilizumab in those with GC-dependent PMR, requiring doses of prednisolone ≥ 10 mg per day [ ]. A total of 101 patients were randomly assigned to receive tocilizumab at a dose of 8 mg/kg every 4 weeks or placebo every 4 weeks, with both groups undergoing a predefined standardised tapering of orally administered prednisolone [ ]. The primary outcome of a CRP-PMR-AS < 10, in addition to attainment of a prednisolone dose of 5 mg per day or a reduction in prednisolone dose by 10 mg from baseline at week 24, was achieved in 67.3% of those in the tocilizumab group compared to 31.4% in the placebo group ( p < 0.001) [ ]; 49% of patients in the tocilizumab arm were no longer receiving GCs at 24 weeks compared to 19.6% in the placebo arm ( p < 0.001) [ ]. Investigational Targeted Therapies Anti-Tumour Necrosis Factor Alpha Agents Early observational studies suggested potential efficacy of tumour necrosis factor alpha (TNFα) antagonists in PMR [ , ]. However, two subsequent phase 3 RCTs failed to confirm a meaningful therapeutic effect (Table ) [ , ]. The largest of these RCTs investigated infliximab, a chimeric monoclonal anti-TNFα antibody, in 51 newly diagnosed, GC-naïve patients with PMR [ ]. Participants were randomised to receive either intravenously administered infliximab (3 mg/kg) or placebo, in combination with a 16-week GC taper [ ]. At 52 weeks, there was no significant difference in the primary endpoint (proportion of patients relapse free) between groups [ ]. Secondary outcomes, including the number and duration of relapses, in addition to cumulative GC exposure were also comparable [ ]. A smaller phase 3 RCT evaluated etanercept, a recombinant human TNF dimeric receptor fusion protein, at a dose of 25 mg subcutaneously biweekly or placebo, in 20 newly diagnosed patients with PMR [ ]. Patients did not receive any GCs in either group, and after 14 days, the PMR-AS score decreased by 24% from baseline ( p = 0.01) in the etanercept group; however, the score remained unchanged in the placebo group ( p > 0.05) [ ]. Given the modest improvement only with etanercept, and the failure of infliximab to meet its primary endpoint, no further studies are currently planned to examine TNFα antagonists in PMR. Nonetheless, important limitations should be acknowledged. Both RCTs were small in scale and the etanercept trial had an exceptionally short follow-up of only 14 days [ ]. Moreover, both studies evaluated the use of anti-TNFα agents in new-onset PMR, and as such, their use in established refractory PMR remains unknown, and may warrant further investigation. This is also supported by the findings of the BRIDGE-PMR RCT and its 1-year extension study, which demonstrated that B cell depletion with rituximab, an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, may be effective in treating PMR (Table ) [ ]. This proof-of-concept 21-week RCT demonstrated the benefit of a single 1-g dose of rituximab, in addition to a 17-week prednisolone taper, in achieving GC-free remission at 21 weeks (48% in rituximab group versus 21% in the placebo group; p = 0.049) in both newly diagnosed patients and those with refractory PMR [ ]. In the 1-year extension study, 47% of those in the rituximab group versus 23% in the placebo group ( p = 0.12) remained in GC-free remission at 52 weeks following the initial single 1-g dose of rituximab [ ]. Janus Kinase Inhibitors The Janus kinase (JAK) family of intracellular tyrosine kinases, which comprises JAK1, JAK2, JAK3 and tyrosine kinase (TYK) 2, in association with signal transducers and activators of transcription (STAT) have a pivotal role in mediating the downstream signalling of a significant number of proinflammatory cytokines. Subsequently, the role of the JAK/STAT pathway and its targeted inhibition using orally administered small molecule JAK inhibitors (JAKi) has garnered much interest in the management of immune-mediated rheumatic diseases, and recently PMR (Table ). Baricitinib, which is a JAK1 and JAK2 inhibitor, exerts a rapid dose-dependent inhibition of IL-6-induced STAT3 phosphorylation, therefore halting the entire subsequent inflammation cascade. Baricitinib was evaluated in the treatment of recent-onset PMR (< 6 months) in the BACHELOR trial, a phase 2, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study [ ]. The primary outcome of the study was the attainment of low disease activity, defined as PMR-AS ≤ 10 at week 12, notably without the use of oral GCs. Fourteen (78%) of 18 participants in the baricitinib group achieved this primary outcome compared with 2 (13%) of 15 participants in the placebo group (relative risk 5.8, 95% CI 3.2–10.6; adjusted p < 0.0001) [ ]. The difference in response between the two groups was observed as early as week 2. After week 12, baricitinib dose was reduced from 4 to 2 mg or placebo, for a further 12 weeks, and treatment response was maintained in 16 (89%) of 18 participants. Baricitinib was discontinued at week 24, and during the observational period up to 36 weeks, there were no disease flares. Although promising, these findings require validation in a phase 3 trial, which is currently ongoing (“JAK-SPARE1” EudraCT2020-005081-34). This is particularly important considering that, although patients were required to be GC free in the 2 weeks prior to enrolment, there was no restriction on GC use before this period, and data on cumulative GC exposure prior to enrolment were not reported. Additionally, it should be noted that the trial design permitted subdeltoid GC injections at week 1 and 4, which could have influenced outcomes. Similarly, in the “EAST PMR”, a single-centre, open-label RCT, tofacitinib, a JAK1–3 inhibitor, at 5 mg twice daily, was evaluated as a monotherapy versus oral GCs in treatment-naïve patients with PMR [ ]. At 24 weeks, there was no statistically significant difference in primary outcome between each group, with all patients in both groups achieving a PMR-AS ≤ 10 at 12 and 24 weeks [ ]. Antibody Drug Conjugates A recent phase 2, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT (AIM-PMR study; NCT04972968 ) evaluated a novel antibody–drug conjugate ABBV-154, comprised of adalimumab (a human monoclonal anti-TNFα antagonist) conjugated to a GC receptor modulator (GRM) [ ]. This was developed to mitigate systemic GC-related adverse effects by selectively delivering the GRM to cells that express transmembrane TNF, including activated immune cells [ ]. In total, 181 patients with GC-dependent, refractory PMR were randomised 1:1:1:1 to placebo ( n = 50) or ABBV-154 at 40 mg ( n = 42), 150 mg ( n = 45) or 340 mg ( n = 44) alongside a standardised GC taper [ ]. The primary efficacy endpoint was time to disease flare. The trial was voluntarily terminated early by the sponsor at week 24, as interim analysis determined that the benefit-risk profile did not sufficiently differentiate ABBV-154 from other currently available therapies for PMR. Nonetheless, time to flare at week 24 favoured the ABBV-154 cohort compared to placebo with dose-responsive hazard ratios (HRs): 40 mg, HR 0.49 (95% CI 0.27–0.88; p = 0.017); 150 mg, HR 0.44 (95% CI 0.25–0.79; p = 0.006); 340 mg, HR 0.20 (95% CI 0.09–0.42; p < 0.001) [ ]. Moreover, incidences of treatment emergent adverse events were similar between groups [ ]. Although these findings suggest potential GC-sparing efficacy, interpretation is limited by early termination, reduced exposure time and sample size. Overall, ABBV-154 provides a proof of concept for antibody–drug conjugates in PMR, but confirmatory, adequately powered trials would be required to define clinical utility. Future Perspectives in the Management of PMR While significant strides have been made over the past decade in the management of isolated PMR, in particular the FDA approval of the first biologic therapy, sarilumab for use in refractory disease, substantial uncertainties remain. Relative to PMRs prevalence, associated disability and significant impact on HRQoL, the progress in management remains inadequate. Indeed, the research agenda and knowledge gaps continue to expand, highlighting persistent knowledge gaps across diagnosis, disease monitoring and optimal treatment strategies. The precise role of the rheumatologist in the care of those with PMR is an ongoing matter of debate. Whilst the importance of specialist evaluation and the benefit of rapid access referral pathways are clear, the practicalities of increased resources for PMR in an already strained rheumatology workforce remain uncertain. However, with an increasing number of biologic agents under evaluation, and the anticipated evolving therapeutic landscape, the need for specialist input will become even more relevant. More studies evaluating the utility, feasibility and cost-effectiveness of early specialist input with rapid access services in ensuring enhanced short- and long-term outcomes including an accurate diagnosis, instigation of appropriate early therapy, stratification for GC sparing agents as appropriate and minimisation of GC-related adverse events are required. However, in order to optimise the role of the rheumatologist, there is an urgent need for the development of a disease stratification tool. However, in order to optimise the role of the rheumatologist, there is an urgent need for the development of a disease stratification tool. In addition to serological or imaging biomarkers, future research should explore the potential of a multimodal prognostication tool including clinical and demographic features, serological and imaging markers, and PROMs. Indeed, the role of PROMs in PMR management needs greater attention in future studies and RCTs. There is a need for clear therapeutic algorithms to guide the management of both early and refractory PMR, along with consensus recommendations for optimal management at each stage of the disease. The potential of a GC-free management in early PMR may be feasible, as demonstrated in the promising results of the BACHELOR RCT [ ]. However, these findings need to be validated in a phase 3 trial, and the roles of other biological therapies in this context also warrant further investigation. Although both biologic agents and JAKi are currently more expensive than oral GCs, the emergence of biosimilars and low cost generics may reduce cost barriers. When considered alongside improved efficacy and safety profiles, particularly in terms of reducing cumulative GC exposure and associated adverse effects, the early, upfront use of these therapies may become a justified and practical approach in future PMR management. Additionally, we know that many GC-dependent patients with PMR are often not considered for management escalation or a GC-sparing agent [ ]. There is perhaps an inertia when the maintenance GC dose is deemed to be relatively low; however, we need to adapt the same standards to GCs in PMR as we do in our other inflammatory rheumatic diseases. The current guidance on monitoring and managing GC-induced adverse events is vague, resulting in much ambiguity and resultant failure to implement appropriate strategies. Finally, there is a need to intensify translational research. Our current understanding of the pathophysiology of PMR is limited, and in order to guide the development and evaluation of targeted therapeutics, greater clarity on the pathogenetic mechanisms is urgently required. Conclusion Despite a recent resurgence of interest in PMR within the rheumatology community and literature, isolated PMR management remains underrepresented in the research landscape compared to other immune-mediated rheumatic disease of a similar prevalence. Critical knowledge gaps persist, particularly in the areas of diagnosis, disease monitoring and long-term management. In this context, we have underscored the importance of early rheumatology input, the development of evidence-based diagnostic tools and prognostic markers, improved monitoring strategies, and approaches to minimise GC exposure and associated adverse effects. With the expanding therapeutic horizon, including the emergence of effective GC-sparing agents, these priorities are increasingly relevant to improve overall outcomes in those with PMR.
